justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias anchored around the prevailing price level of the S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which was trading in the mid-to-high 480s at the time of the forecast. For the one-day horizon, I set the estimate close to the then-current price, reflecting the well-documented near-random-walk behavior of equity indices over very short horizons and a slight upward drift assumption consistent with historical daily returns. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the figure slightly higher to incorporate the small but positive expected return over that window. For the one-month horizon, the point estimate climbs modestly further, consistent with annualized equity risk premium expectations translated into a roughly 1–2% expected gain over a month, absent any strong macro signals pointing decisively in either direction.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect realized and implied volatility at each horizon. At the one-day level, the interval is relatively tight because daily moves in SPY tend to cluster in a modest range under normal market conditions — a roughly 1% standard deviation for a single session. As the horizon extends to one week and then one month, uncertainty compounds, and the intervals widen accordingly. The one-month interval in particular reflects the well-known square-root-of-time scaling of volatility, as well as the possibility that within a month, multiple macro data releases, Federal Reserve communications, and earnings reports could each independently move the market by meaningful amounts.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve policy signaling — either a hawkish surprise that drives rates sharply higher or an unexpected pivot that sparks a rally. Geopolitical escalation, particularly in regions affecting energy supply chains, could also produce sharp downside moves. On the upside, a materially stronger-than-expected economic data print or a resolution of trade tensions could push SPY well above the upper bounds. Liquidity events or a credit market dislocation — less probable but historically impactful — represent tail risks that my intervals do not fully capture by construction, since 90% confidence intervals explicitly leave 10% probability mass in the tails.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that forecast intervals of this type are inherently model-dependent and sensitive to assumptions about return distributions. Equity returns exhibit fat tails and occasional volatility clustering, meaning that real-world extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a simple normal distribution would suggest.
